title: Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy and Power

toc.title: 2.1 Newton's laws of motion and the conditions of equilibrium
2.2 Impulse, linear momentum and its conservation
2.3 Work, energy and power; the work–energy theorem; conservation of energy
2.5 Solid friction: laws, coefficient, angle of friction and angle of repose

html:
Dynamics asks why bodies move as they do: forces change momentum, forces do work, and work changes energy. Of the 10 Mechanics questions in the Physics paper (official), we estimate about 2 come from this chapter. They are built on a few patterns that repeat year after year: the reading of a weighing machine in a lift, recoil of a gun, impulse from a force–time graph, the link K = p^2/2m, power of a pump or a vehicle, velocities after a collision, and friction on a level road or an inclined plane.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Newton's laws: inertia, F = dp/dt, action–reaction on different bodies; free-body diagrams.
  • Apparent weight in a lift, connected bodies and the Atwood machine; Lami's theorem for three forces in equilibrium.
  • Impulse = change in momentum = area under the F–t graph; conservation of momentum (recoil, explosions, rockets).
  • W = Fs\cos\theta; work–energy theorem; K = p^2/2m; conservation of mechanical energy; P = Fv.
  • Collisions: elastic and inelastic, coefficient of restitution, equal-mass exchange, kinetic-energy loss.
  • Friction: f \le \mu_sN, f_k = \mu_kN, \mu_s = \tan\theta_{repose}, motion on rough inclines.

2.1 Newton's laws of motion and the conditions of equilibrium

The three laws

Law Statement What it gives
First (law of inertia) A body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless an external net force acts on it. The idea of inertia and a qualitative definition of force; defines inertial frames
Second The rate of change of momentum is proportional to the net external force and takes place in its direction: \vec F = \frac{d\vec p}{dt}. F = ma for constant mass; 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²
Third To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces come in pairs, acting on two different bodies

Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform motion; mass is its measure. There is inertia of rest (passengers jerk back when a bus starts), of motion (they lurch forward when it brakes) and of direction (they lean outward on a bend).

The first law is contained in the second (put F = 0, then a = 0), and the second contains the third's consequence, conservation of momentum. For a system whose mass changes at a steady speed, F = v\,\frac{dm}{dt} — the force needed to keep a conveyor belt moving at speed v while sand drops onto it, or the thrust of a rocket that ejects gas at relative speed u: F = u\,\frac{dm}{dt}.

Action and reaction never cancel

They act on different bodies. A book on a table: the weight of the book (Earth pulls book) and the normal reaction (table pushes book) are equal and opposite and act on the same body — they balance, but they are not an action–reaction pair. The reaction to the book's weight is the book pulling the Earth upward.

Standard applications

Situation Result
Lift accelerating up at a (or moving down and slowing) apparent weight R = m(g + a)
Lift accelerating down at a (or moving up and slowing) R = m(g - a)
Lift at rest or moving at constant velocity R = mg
Lift falling freely (a = g) R = 0 — weightlessness
Atwood machine, masses m_1 > m_2 over a light frictionless pulley a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2}, T = \frac{2m_1m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}
Two blocks in contact on a smooth floor, force F on m_1 a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}; contact force = \frac{m_2F}{m_1 + m_2}
Block on a smooth incline of angle \theta a = g\sin\theta down the slope; N = mg\cos\theta

The direction of velocity never matters for a weighing machine; only the direction of the acceleration does.

Worked example 2.1 — lift and Atwood machine

Problem. (a) A 60 kg student stands on a weighing machine in a lift that accelerates upward at 2 m s⁻². What does the machine read? (b) Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang over a light frictionless pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension (g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}).

Solution. (a) R = m(g + a) = 60(9.8 + 2) = 708\ \text{N} (it "reads" 72.2 kg). (b) a = (3 - 2)(9.8)/5 = 1.96\ \text{m s}^{-2}; T = 2(3)(2)(9.8)/5 = 23.5\ \text{N} — between the two weights (19.6 N and 29.4 N), as it must be.

Conditions of equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when it has no linear acceleration and no angular acceleration.

  1. Translational equilibrium: the vector sum of all external forces is zero, \sum\vec F = 0 (so \sum F_x = 0, \sum F_y = 0).
  2. Rotational equilibrium: the sum of the moments (torques) about any point is zero, \sum\tau = 0 — the principle of moments: clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments.

A point object needs only the first; a rigid body needs both. A couple (two equal, opposite, parallel forces not in line) has zero resultant force but a non-zero torque, so it rotates the body without translating it.

Lami's theorem. If three concurrent, coplanar forces P, Q, R keep a body in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two:

\frac{P}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R}{\sin\gamma}

where \alpha is the angle between Q and R, and so on. Three forces in equilibrium can be drawn as a closed triangle (forces 3 N, 4 N and 5 N in equilibrium: the 3 N and 4 N forces are at 90°).

Worked example 2.2 — a lamp on a wire

Problem. A 20 N lamp hangs from the midpoint of a wire; the two halves of the wire make 120° with each other. Find the tension in each half.

Solution. Each half makes 60° with the vertical. Vertical balance: 2T\cos60^{\circ} = 20, so T = 20\ \text{N}. (As the wire is pulled straighter, the angle approaches 180°, \cos of the half-angle approaches zero and T grows without limit — a wire carrying a load can never be made perfectly horizontal.)

Type of equilibrium After a small displacement Potential energy Example
Stable returns minimum cone on its base, ball in a bowl
Unstable moves further away maximum cone on its tip
Neutral stays in the new position constant cone on its side, ball on a level floor

2.2 Impulse, linear momentum and its conservation

Linear momentum \vec p = m\vec v (vector, kg m s⁻¹). Impulse of a force is \vec J = \vec F\,\Delta t for a constant force, or \int\vec F\,dt in general; by the second law it equals the change in momentum:

\vec J = \int \vec F\,dt = \vec p_f - \vec p_i = \Delta\vec p

Impulse is the area under the force–time graph; its unit, N s, equals kg m s⁻¹. For a given change of momentum, a longer contact time means a smaller average force — the physics of a cricketer drawing the hands back, airbags, crumple zones, the sand pit for long jump, and shock absorbers.

Useful results.

  • A ball of mass m hitting a wall normally at speed v and rebounding at the same speed: |\Delta p| = 2mv (not zero). At angle \theta to the wall's normal: 2mv\cos\theta.
  • A machine gun firing n bullets per second, each of mass m at speed v, pushes back on the gunner with force F = nmv.
  • Kinetic energy and momentum: K = \frac{p^2}{2m}, p = \sqrt{2mK}. For the same momentum the lighter body has more KE; for the same KE the heavier body has more momentum.
Principle of conservation of linear momentum

If the net external force on a system is zero, its total linear momentum stays constant: m_1\vec u_1 + m_2\vec u_2 = m_1\vec v_1 + m_2\vec v_2. Internal forces (action–reaction pairs inside the system) cannot change the total.

Application What is conserved and what follows
Recoil of a gun 0 = mv + MV, so V = -mv/M; the bullet carries far more KE (K_b/K_g = M/m)
Explosion of a shell at rest fragments fly apart with momenta that add to zero
Rocket and jet propulsion gases pushed backward, rocket pushed forward; thrust = u\,dm/dt
Person jumping off a boat boat moves backward
Collisions total momentum before = total momentum after (Section 2.4)
Worked example 2.3 — recoil and impulse

Problem. (a) A 5 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 500 m s⁻¹. Find the recoil speed and the ratio of the kinetic energies of bullet and rifle. (b) A 0.15 kg ball reaches a bat at 20 m s⁻¹ and leaves along the same line at 30 m s⁻¹; contact lasts 0.01 s. Find the average force.

Solution. (a) V = mv/M = 0.02(500)/5 = 2\ \text{m s}^{-1}, backward. Equal momenta, so K \propto 1/m: K_b/K_g = 5/0.02 = 250. (b) Take the final direction as positive: \Delta p = 0.15(30) - 0.15(-20) = 7.5\ \text{N s}; F = 7.5/0.01 = 750\ \text{N}. Forgetting the reversal (using 30 - 20) gives the wrong 150 N.

2.3 Work, energy and power; the work–energy theorem; conservation of energy

Work

The work done by a constant force is the scalar product of force and displacement:

W = \vec F\cdot\vec s = Fs\cos\theta

Unit: joule (1 J = 1 N m); dimensions [ML^2T^{-2}].

Sign When Examples
Positive (0 \le \theta < 90^{\circ}) force has a component along the motion gravity on a falling body; the engine force on a car
Zero (\theta = 90^{\circ}, or no displacement) force perpendicular to motion centripetal force in a circle; a porter carrying a load on a level road (against gravity); pushing a wall
Negative (90^{\circ} < \theta \le 180^{\circ}) force opposes the motion kinetic friction; gravity on a body being lifted; brakes

For a variable force, W = \int F\,dx = area under the force–displacement graph. For a spring obeying F = kx, the work to stretch it from x_1 to x_2 is \frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2) — from 0 to x it is \frac{1}{2}kx^2.

Energy and the work–energy theorem

Kinetic energy K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2; gravitational potential energy near the Earth U = mgh; elastic potential energy of a spring U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2.

Work–energy theorem

The work done by the net force on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_{net} = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2. It holds for any force, constant or variable, conservative or not.

A conservative force does work that depends only on the start and end points, not on the path; its work round any closed path is zero, and a potential energy can be defined for it (gravity, the spring force, the electrostatic force). Friction, air drag and viscous forces are non-conservative (dissipative): their work depends on the path and turns mechanical energy into heat.

Conservation of mechanical energy. If only conservative forces do work, K + U = constant. A body sliding down any smooth track of height h reaches the bottom with v = \sqrt{2gh}, whatever the shape of the track. With friction, K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f + (\text{work against friction}). The law of conservation of energy — energy is neither created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another — has no exceptions (mass is a form of energy, E = mc^2).

Power

Power is the rate of doing work: P = \frac{dW}{dt}; for a force on a moving body P = \vec F\cdot\vec v = Fv\cos\theta. Unit: watt (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹); dimensions [ML^2T^{-3}]. 1 horsepower (hp) ≈ 746 W. The kilowatt hour is a unit of energy: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (one "unit" on an NEA bill). Efficiency = useful output / input.

Worked example 2.4 — pump and vehicle

Problem. (a) A motor pumps 600 kg of water into a tank 20 m above it in 2 min. Find the minimum power (g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}). (b) A car's engine delivers 30 kW. The total resistance on a level road is 1500 N. Find the car's top speed.

Solution. (a) P = mgh/t = 600(9.8)(20)/120 = 980\ \text{W} (more in practice, since the water also leaves with kinetic energy and the motor is not 100 % efficient). (b) At top speed the driving force equals the resistance, so v = P/F = 30\,000/1500 = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1} = 72\ \text{km h}^{-1}.

Momentum and kinetic energy change differently

K = p^2/2m, so K \propto p^2. If p increases by 50 %, K becomes 1.5^2 = 2.25 times — an increase of 125 %, not 50 % or 100 %. If K increases by 300 % (four times), p doubles — an increase of 100 %.

2.4 Elastic and inelastic collisions

In every collision of an isolated system linear momentum is conserved and total energy is conserved; what may not be conserved is kinetic energy (part can become heat, sound or deformation).

Elastic Inelastic Perfectly inelastic
Momentum conserved conserved conserved
Kinetic energy conserved not conserved (some lost) not conserved (maximum loss)
After impact separate separate move together (stick)
Coefficient of restitution e e = 1 0 < e < 1 e = 0
Examples collisions of atoms, molecules; nearly, of steel or billiard balls most real collisions bullet embedding in a block, mud on a wall

The coefficient of restitution is the ratio of the relative speed of separation to the relative speed of approach (head-on):

e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}

Elastic collision in one dimension

For m_1 at u_1 striking m_2 at u_2 head-on and elastically:

v_1 = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)u_1 + 2m_2u_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \qquad v_2 = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)u_2 + 2m_1u_1}{m_1 + m_2}

Special case (target at rest, u_2 = 0) Result
Equal masses the bodies exchange velocities: v_1 = 0, v_2 = u_1
Very heavy body hits a very light one heavy continues at \approx u_1; light flies off at \approx 2u_1
Very light body hits a very heavy one light rebounds at \approx -u_1; heavy hardly moves
Fraction of KE given to the target \frac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2} — 100 % when m_1 = m_2

This last row is why a moderator in a reactor uses light nuclei (hydrogen in water, deuterium in heavy water, carbon in graphite) to slow neutrons: a neutron loses most energy when it hits a nucleus of nearly its own mass. In an oblique elastic collision of two equal masses, one at rest, the two move off at 90° to each other.

Perfectly inelastic collision

The bodies move off together with v = \frac{m_1u_1 + m_2u_2}{m_1 + m_2}. The kinetic energy lost is \frac{m_1m_2(u_1 - u_2)^2}{2(m_1 + m_2)}; with the target at rest the fraction lost is \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2} (one half for equal masses).

Ballistic pendulum: a bullet of mass m embeds in a block of mass M that then swings up a height h: v_{bullet} = \frac{m + M}{m}\sqrt{2gh} (momentum conserved in the impact, energy conserved in the swing — never energy in the impact).

Bouncing ball: dropped from height h onto a floor with coefficient e, it rises to e^2h; after n bounces, e^{2n}h; and e = \sqrt{h_2/h_1}.

Worked example 2.5 — elastic and sticking collisions

Problem. A 2 kg trolley at 3 m s⁻¹ hits a 1 kg trolley at rest. Find the velocities after impact if the collision is (a) elastic, (b) perfectly inelastic, and (c) the kinetic energy lost in (b).

Solution. (a) v_1 = \frac{(2 - 1)3}{3} = 1\ \text{m s}^{-1} and v_2 = \frac{2(2)(3)}{3} = 4\ \text{m s}^{-1}. Check: momentum 6 = 2 + 4; KE 9 = 1 + 8 J. (b) v = 6/3 = 2\ \text{m s}^{-1}. (c) KE before 9 J, after \frac{1}{2}(3)(2^2) = 6 J: 3 J lost, which is the fraction \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{1}{3}.

2.5 Solid friction: laws, coefficient, angle of friction and angle of repose

Friction is the force that opposes relative motion (or attempted motion) between two surfaces in contact; it acts along the surfaces. It arises from the interlocking of surface irregularities and the adhesion at the tiny points of true contact.

  • Static friction acts when there is no sliding. It is self-adjusting: it is exactly as large as needed to prevent slipping, up to a maximum.
  • Limiting friction is that maximum, reached just as sliding begins: f_s = \mu_sN.
  • Kinetic (dynamic) friction acts during sliding: f_k = \mu_kN, with \mu_k < \mu_s.
  • Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction — the reason for wheels and ball bearings.

Laws of limiting friction

  1. Friction acts along the common surface, opposite to the (attempted) relative motion.
  2. Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction: f_s = \mu_sN.
  3. It is independent of the apparent area of contact (for the same normal reaction).
  4. It depends on the nature and condition of the surfaces (material, roughness, lubrication).
  5. Kinetic friction is nearly independent of the speed (for moderate speeds) and is less than limiting friction.

The coefficient of friction \mu = f/N is a dimensionless ratio. It is usually below 1 but can exceed 1 for very clean or sticky surfaces (rubber on dry road).

Angle of friction and angle of repose

  • Angle of friction \lambda: the angle that the resultant of the limiting friction and the normal reaction makes with the normal reaction: \tan\lambda = \frac{f_s}{N} = \mu_s.
  • Angle of repose \theta_r: the smallest angle of an inclined plane at which a body placed on it just begins to slide down. At that angle mg\sin\theta_r = \mu_s\,mg\cos\theta_r, so \mu_s = \tan\theta_r.

Hence angle of repose = angle of friction, and neither depends on the mass of the body. (Sand piles, scree slopes in the hills and grain heaps settle at their angle of repose.)

Friction in calculations

Situation Result
Block sliding on a rough level floor deceleration \mu_kg; stopping distance \frac{u^2}{2\mu_kg} (independent of mass)
Block sliding down a rough incline (\theta > \theta_r) a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)
Block slides down at constant velocity \mu_k = \tan\theta
Pushing a block up an incline at steady speed F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)
Least force (along the incline) that stops it sliding down F = mg(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)
Pulling at angle \alpha above the horizontal N = mg - F\sin\alpha (less friction)
Pushing at angle \alpha below the horizontal N = mg + F\sin\alpha (more friction)

So it is easier to pull a lawn roller than to push it. Friction is not only a nuisance: walking, the grip of tyres, brakes, belts on pulleys and writing all depend on it. It is reduced by polishing, lubrication, ball bearings and streamlining.

Worked example 2.6 — rough incline and braking

Problem. (a) A block slides down an incline with \sin\theta = 0.6 and \mu_k = 0.25. Find its acceleration (g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}). (b) A car at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes with its wheels locked on a road with \mu_k = 0.5. Find the stopping distance.

Solution. (a) \cos\theta = 0.8; a = 10(0.6 - 0.25\times0.8) = 4\ \text{m s}^{-2}. (b) s = u^2/(2\mu_kg) = 400/10 = 40\ \text{m}. Double the speed and it becomes 160 m.

Friction questions in 30 seconds

First decide whether the body moves. Compare the applied force (or mg\sin\theta) with the limiting friction \mu_sN. If it is smaller, the body stays at rest and the friction equals the applied force — not \mu N. A 10 kg box with \mu_s = 0.5 pushed with 20 N on a level floor feels 20 N of friction, not 49 N.

Trap — action and reaction never cancel on the same body

The third-law pair always acts on two different bodies, so the forces never appear in the same free-body diagram and never "cancel out". A horse pulls a cart because the ground pushes the horse (reaction to the horse pushing the ground backwards). Neighbouring traps: the normal reaction of a surface is not the reaction to the body's weight (weight is the Earth pulling the body; its pair is the body pulling the Earth), and in an inelastic collision kinetic energy is lost but momentum is still conserved provided no external impulse acts.

Chapter summary

  • Inertia is resistance to change of motion, measured by mass; \vec F = d\vec p/dt; action and reaction are equal, opposite and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.
  • A weighing machine reads m(g \pm a) according to the direction of the acceleration; zero in free fall, mg at constant velocity.
  • Equilibrium of a rigid body needs zero net force and zero net torque; three concurrent forces in equilibrium obey Lami's theorem.
  • Impulse = change in momentum = area under the force–time graph; spreading the same impulse over more time lowers the force.
  • With no external force, total momentum is conserved: recoil, explosions, rockets and every collision.
  • W = Fs\cos\theta; the net work equals the change in kinetic energy; K = p^2/2m; P = Fv.
  • Elastic collisions conserve KE (e = 1); perfectly inelastic ones stick together (e = 0) and lose the most KE; equal masses in an elastic head-on collision exchange velocities.
  • Limiting friction \mu_sN is independent of area of contact; \mu_k < \mu_s; angle of repose = angle of friction, \mu_s = \tan\theta_r.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — the first law says a body keeps its state unless a net force acts: the property of resisting change is inertia (measured by mass).

2. (b) — impulse = force × time, N s, the same as kg m s⁻¹ (the unit of momentum). N m is the unit of work or torque.

3. (c) — the third-law pair acts on two different bodies, so the forces cannot cancel; they are equal at every instant, whatever the motion.

4. (d) — zero net force gives no linear acceleration; zero net torque gives no angular acceleration. A rigid body needs both.

5. (a) — the centripetal force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, so W = Fs\cos90^{\circ} = 0; the speed does not change.

6. (b) — W = \int F\,dx is the area under F–x. Impulse is the area under F–t.

7. (c) — \int F\,dt = impulse = change in momentum.

8. (d) — K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{(mv)^2}{2m} = \frac{p^2}{2m}.

9. (a) — the work of gravity depends only on the change in height, not on the path; friction, air drag and viscous forces dissipate energy.

10. (b) — 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; the kWh is a unit of energy, not power.

11. (c) — momentum is conserved in every collision; in a perfectly inelastic one the bodies stick together and the loss of KE is the greatest.

12. (d) — e = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach = 1 when no KE is lost.

13. (b) — with m_1 = m_2 and u_2 = 0, the formulas give v_1 = 0 and v_2 = u_1: the velocities are exchanged (as in billiards).

14. (c) — at the angle of repose mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta, so \mu_s = \tan\theta.

15. (b) — the third law of friction: for the same normal reaction, the area of contact does not matter. Friction is proportional to N, so (d) is wrong.

16. (a) — \mu_k < \mu_s: it takes more force to start sliding than to keep sliding.

17. (c) — bearings replace sliding with rolling, and rolling friction is far smaller; friction is reduced, not removed.

18. (d) — W_{net} = \Delta K. Work by conservative forces alone equals -\Delta U, which is a different statement.

19. (a) — in free fall both the man and the machine accelerate at g, so R = m(g - g) = 0: apparent weightlessness.

20. (b) — the exhaust gases are pushed backward and the rocket gains equal forward momentum (equivalently, Newton's third law); kinetic energy is not conserved.

21. (d) — 1 hp ≈ 746 W.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — uniform velocity means zero acceleration, so R = mg. Only acceleration changes the reading, never the direction of motion alone.

2. (b) — the change in momentum (impulse) is fixed by the catch; lengthening the contact time reduces the average force F = \Delta p/\Delta t.

3. (a) — p = \sqrt{2mK}; with equal K, p \propto \sqrt{m}: \sqrt{1} : \sqrt{4} = 1 : 2.

4. (d) — momentum goes from +mv to -mv, a change of 2mv; it is zero only for speed, not for the vector momentum.

5. (a) — total momentum stays zero, so the momenta are equal and opposite; with equal p, K = p^2/2m is larger for the lighter bullet (by the ratio M/m).

6. (b) — the upward component of the pull reduces the normal reaction (N = mg - F\sin\alpha), so the friction \mu N is less; pushing adds to N.

7. (c) — with m_1 \gg m_2, v_2 = 2m_1u_1/(m_1 + m_2) \approx 2u.

8. (a) — his upward force on the load is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so the work against gravity is zero (he still tires, but that is not work on the load).

9. (c) — K \propto p^2: 1.5^2 = 2.25, so K rises by 125 %.

10. (d) — \mu_s = \tan30^{\circ} = 1/\sqrt{3} \approx 0.58. 0.50 is \sin30^{\circ} and 0.87 is \cos30^{\circ}.

11. (a) — constant velocity means zero net force: mg\sin\theta = \mu_kmg\cos\theta, so \mu_k = \tan\theta.

12. (c) — the rebound speed is e times the impact speed, and height \propto v^2: h' = e^2h = 0.25h.

13. (d) — the belt must give the arriving sand momentum at the rate v\,dm/dt, so F = dp/dt = v\,dm/dt.

14. (b) — in equilibrium the three forces form a closed triangle with sides 3, 4, 5, a right-angled triangle, so the 3 N and 4 N forces are perpendicular.

Answers and explanations — Set C

1. (d) — the velocity reverses: \Delta p = 0.15(30 + 20) = 7.5 N s; F = 7.5/0.01 = 750 N. (a) forgets the reversal (uses 30 − 20).

2. (a) — momentum conservation: V = mv/M = 0.010(400)/4 = 1 m s⁻¹, opposite to the bullet.

3. (b) — moving down and slowing down means the acceleration is upward: R = m(g + a) = 50(12) = 600 N. (a) wrongly uses g - a.

6. (d) — perfectly inelastic: v = mu/(m + M) = 0.01(300)/1.00 = 3 m s⁻¹. (c) forgets to add the bullet's mass to the block.

10. (b) — W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2) = 100(0.04 - 0.01) = 3 J. (a) is the work for the first 10 cm, and (c) the work from 0 to 20 cm.
